title: Does a greater training load increase the risk of injury and illness in ultramarathon runners? A prospective, descriptive, longitudinal design
authors: Craddock N, Buchholtz K, Burgess TL
journal: South African Journal of Sports Medicine
population: 119 runners training for the 2019 Two Oceans ultramarathon (56 km), weekly online logbook over 16 weeks
findings: Injury incidence was 5 per 1,000 training hours; illness incidence was 16 per 1,000 training days.
There was a significant relationship between external training load and injury and illness incidence for runners who ran less than 30 km per week.
There was a significant relationship between the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) and injury incidence when ACWR was > 1.5, and with illness incidence when ACWR was < 0.5.
The authors recommend monitoring both absolute and relative workloads.
limitations: One 56-km race, 119 self-reporting runners, no effect sizes in the abstract; conflicts with [burgess-2025-training-load-injury-gam] on ACWR; ACWR methodology is itself contested.
implications: Show a low-volume note when average weekly distance is under 30 km in the 12 weeks before an ultra (one study, low confidence).
Treat ACWR > 1.5 as an informational caution, not a hard gate, because the later 90-km cohort found minimal ACWR effect.

verification.notes: Added in this review: the researcher cited this paper inside the Burgess entry but described it as a Comrades cohort; Europe PMC and Crossref show it is a Two Oceans (56 km) study of 119 runners.
